## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

The manuscript by Lin et al. presents compelling experimental evidence of coupling between quantum Hall (QH) plasmons and a double quantum dot system. This is a novel and intriguing result with potential implications for hybrid quantum systems, especially in contexts where topologically protected modes are desirable. The topic is timely and of high relevance for the quantum technologies community. I am inclined to support publication, but I have several concerns and requests for clarification that I believe must be addressed before proceeding:
1) One of the core features of quantum Hall edge modes is their chirality. It is not entirely clear how this feature is impacting the results of this work. Specifically:
a. In the Methods section, Eq. (3) describes a potential that appears to be that of a standing wave. This seems inconsistent with the absence of counter-propagating modes in a chiral system. Maybe is it possible that phi_0 is itself time-dependent and encodes the chiral propagation? If so, this should be made more explicit. If not, what defines phi_0 and how does the formulation account for unidirectional propagation?
b. More generally, how does chirality manifest in the coupling between the edge and the double quantum dots? I can imagine that this could impact coupling of more that one double dot
2) Could the authors clarify whether parasitic capacitances have been included in the model and how they might affect the plasmon propagation? As shown in Mahoney et al., Phys. Rev. X 7, 011007 (2017), such capacitances can even reverse the effective chirality of the signal propagation. A brief discussion or estimate of their effect in this geometry would we helpful.
3) Is it possible to tune the plasmon velocity at fixed magnetic field via gate voltages on the coupling gates? Intuitively, one could imagine that adjusting the electrostatic environment could alter the local capacitance per unit length or the confinement profile, and thereby modify the plasmon dispersion. Have the authors explored this experimentally?
4) The capacitance to the gates and ground planes is likely non-uniform along the edge. How does this spatial variation affect the plasmon-dot coupling? Could this be used to optimize the placement of the quantum dot for enhanced coupling?
5) While demonstrating plasmon-double dot coupling is a significant step, the coupling strength reported here is relatively modest compared to state-of-the-art charge-photon coupling rates, which can be substantially above the 100 MHz range (e.g., Samkharadze et al., Science 359, 1123 (2018); de Palma et al., Nat. Commun. 15, 2703 (2024); Yu et al., Nat. Nanotechnol. 18, 1360 (2023)). This is somewhat surprising, especially given the high impedance of QH edge modes. In the Outlook section, the authors suggest possible improvements to increase the coupling, but I believe the paper would benefit significantly from a more quantitative analysis of these prospects. Can the authors provide estimates for how large g could realistically become, and how it compares to coupling in superconducting resonator systems? A more explicit comparison with these technologies could greatly strengthen the relevance of this work.
6) The observed Q factor is quite low. Do the authors attribute this to dielectric losses, residual bulk conduction, edge disorder due to etching, or other mechanisms? The authors mention that this can be solved by higher mobility materials, but could improvements be expected also by defining edges electrostatically rather than through etching?
7) In the Introduction, the authors assert that backscattering is absent in QH systems. While this is true in the DC limit, backscattering can occur at finite frequency, especially at low magnetic fields.
8) The reported dissipation rate gamma is higher than what has been demonstrated in other GaAs samples (e.g., a few MHz as in reference 15). Could the authors comment on whether this elevated dissipation is an artifact of the device geometry, the fabrication method (e.g., etched edges), or other limitations?
9) The coupling strength g is sometimes provided in frequency but its equations are in energy. Good to specify if the extracted values of g are divided by h or hbar.

### Reviewer 2

In the article entitled “Dispersive detection of a charge qubit with a broadband high-impedance quantum-Hall plasmon resonator”, Lin and cowokers explore circuit quantum electrodynamics with plasmonic resonators formed by the edge states of a closed quantum Hall droplet. The authors couple a plasmonic resonator to a double quantum dot operated as a charge qubit. Analyzing the phase response of the resonator within the standard framework of the Jaynes-Cumming model (dispersive regime), the authors extract the qubit properties (decoherence rate, spectrum) for different gate voltages. The authors also investigate how the power sent in the input probe tone affects the resonator response.
Overall, the paper reads easily. The analysis of the results is sound and the experimental data are in rather good agreement with the theoretical models derived. In my opinion, the data and the analysis support the main claim of the manuscript that is the dispersive detection of a semiconductor charge qubit with a quantum Hall resonator. This work provides a new alternative platform for circuit quantum electrodynamics. To my knowledge, this represents the first demonstration of the use of a quantum Hall plasmonic resonator in such experiments and this is the main novelty of this work. This work could interest a broad community of researchers in the field of mesoscopic quantum physics, in particular those working on high-mobility 2D electronic systems. I think it may stimulate theoretical and experimental works on the use quantum Hall resonators as probing tools, in particular in the context of fractional quantum (anomalous) Hall effect.
Despite this, I think the authors should further motivate their work and further highlight the perspectives it offers. I also have few concerns regarding the future of this platform. Additionally, I have questions regarding some parts of the data analysis and the interpretation of the data. Once these points have been addressed, I could recommend the publication of this manuscript in Nature Communications.
Major questions:
(1) I think standard transport characterizations of the device/heterostructure are missing. Measures of the longitudinal Rxx and transverse Rxy resistances in a Hall bar made on the same sample/heterostructure would allow to evaluate the quality of the quantum Hall states forming at the magnetic field at which the device is operated. In particular, a measure of Rxx at ν = 2 would provide insights on the residual bulk conductivity and thus on the dissipation in the resonator. Do the authors have such a measurement? Can they measure Rxx in a configuration where the central part is open (no resonator formed like in Fig. S1)?
Similarly, the mobility of the GaAs/AlGaAs heterostructure should be reported. This quantity is relevant especially as higher mobility samples should enable the formation of resonators with higher Q as mentioned by the authors.
(2) In my opinion, a more in-depth discussion about the advantages and prospects offered by quantum Hall plasmonic resonators should be carried out. In particular the use of plasmonic resonators instead of high-impedance superconducting resonators (Z0 = 7.9 kOhms in Janik et al., Nat. Comm., 16, 2103 (2025)) should be further motivated. Is the high characteristic impedance the only advantage of quantum Hall plasmonic resonators?
(3) The current quality factor is low Q = 4 and this limits the possibilities offered by the resonator despite offering a large detection bandwidth. As acknowledged by the authors, achieving the strong coupling regime is desirable and one solution is to increase the Q factor. The authors could discuss how the resonator linewidth κ scales with L and v.

### Reviewer 3

The authors report of a system where a charge q-bit (tunnel coupled double quantum dot) is coupled to the plasmon excitation of a Hall edge channel. This system realizes the standard Jaynes -Cumming QED Hamiltonian describing a two-level system coupled with a single boson. The authors perform several experiments which allow to gain information on the q-bit characteristics, by a heterodyne measurement on the transmission through the plasmon channel. In the dispersive regime, they extract the energy levels and coupling strength of the double quantum dots (Fig. 3), and they reconstruct its charge state diagram (Fig. 2). For a nearly resonant condition and by varying the input drive on the plasmon channel, they also estimate the average number of plasmons by measuring the polarization saturation of the double dot.
These types of measurements have been reported before (and a pretty common) form qubits coupled with transmission line resonators; the novelty here is the fact that the boson resonator is provided by the plasmon of an edge Hall state. While such plasmon excitations have been recently reported https://www.nature.com/articles/s42005-024-01803-6, to my knowledge, here the authors report their coupling with a qbit for the first time. Also, the authors work in a regime of high impedance of the plasmon mode, which results in higher coupling strength (although the quality factor is low). These novelty grant publication in Nature communications.
The paper can benefit from minor improvements. For instance, in the second paragraph of page 3 there is a confusion between the plasmon velocity and the Landau filling factor that are noted with the same greek letter “nu”. In general, it is not obvious for an unspecialized reader why the plasmon frequency should scale as the inverse of the magnetic field, while it is independent on the Landau level filling factor. The authors might provide a more detailed explanation on that point. In Figure 1c the transitions between filling factors seems to be correlated to changes in the transmission signal, can the authors comment on that? Finally, do they control the positions of the anti-nodes of of the plamon wave-voltage?

Reply to Reviewer #3’ comments
The authors report of a system where a charge q-bit (tunnel coupled double quantum dot) is coupled to the plasmon excitation of a Hall edge channel. This system realizes the standard Jaynes -Cumming QED Hamiltonian describing a two-level system coupled with a single boson. The authors perform several experiments which allow to gain information on the q-bit characteristics, by a heterodyne measurement on the transmission through the plasmon channel. In the dispersive regime, they extract the energy levels and coupling strength of the double quantum dots (Fig. 3), and they reconstruct its charge state diagram (Fig. 2). For a nearly resonant condition and by varying the input drive on the plasmon channel, they also estimate the average number of plasmons by measuring the polarization saturation of the double dot.
These types of measurements have been reported before (and a pretty common) form qubits coupled with transmission line resonators; the novelty here is the fact that the boson resonator is provided by the plasmon of an edge Hall state. While such plasmon excitations have been recently reported https://www.nature.com/articles/s42005-024-01803-6, to my knowledge, here the authors report their coupling with a qbit for the first time. Also, the authors work in a regime of high impedance of the plasmon mode, which results in higher coupling strength (although the quality factor is low). These novelty grant publication in Nature communications.
